response.query: What is the computational plan to generate 500–1,000 surrogates per window (CPU/GPU allocation, runtime, memory), and what cluster/permutation thresholds and resource contingencies are required?
response.answer: To generate 500-1,000 surrogates per window, allocate 1-2 GPUs per job, request 10-20 CPUs, and set memory limits to 200-400MB per GPU. Ensure cluster defaults are adjusted if needed.

results.title: Allocation of CPU and Memory -
results.content: + Defaults for --cpu-limit flag. + Defaults for --memory-limit flag. When submitting a Job, you can request a guaranteed amount of CPUs and memory by using the **--cpu** and **--memory** flags in the *runai submit* command. You can limit your Job's allocation of CPU and memory by using the **--cpu-limit** and **--memory-limit** flags in the **runai submit** command. The limit (for both CPU and memory) overrides the cluster default described in the section below. The default is cluster-wide and is defined as a **ratio** of GPUs to CPUs. If, for example, the default has been defined as 1:6 and your Job has specified `--gpu 2` and has not specified `--cpu`, then the implied `--cpu` flag value is 12 CPUs. The system comes with a cluster-wide default of 1:1. If you didn't request any GPUs for your job and has not specified `--cpu`, the default is defined as a ratio of CPU limit to CPUs. If, for example, the default has been defined as 1:0.2 and your Job has specified `--cpu-limit 10` and has not specified `--cpu`, then the implied `--cpu` flag value is 2 CPUs. The system comes with a cluster-wide default of 1:0.1. The default is cluster-wide and is proportional to the number of requested GPUs. The system comes with a cluster-wide default of 100MiB of allocated CPU memory per GPU. If you didn't request any GPUs for your job and has not specified `--memory`, the default is defined as a ratio of CPU Memory limit to CPU Memory Request. If your Job has not specified `--cpu-limit`, then by default, the system will not set a limit. If your Job has not specified `--memory-limit`, then by default, the system will not set a limit. * a CPU request with a default ratio of 2:1 CPUs to GPUs. * a CPU Memory request with a default ratio of 200MB per GPU. * a CPU limit with a default ratio of 4:1 CPU to GPU. * a CPU request with a default ratio of 0.1 CPUs per 1 CPU limit. * a CPU Memory request with a default ratio of 0.1:1 request per CPU Memory limit.

results.title: CPU Compute and Memory Allocation | SaaS | Run:ai Documentation
results.content: * If CPU compute and memory are not explicitly requested, resources are assigned from the cluster default. If CPU compute and memory resource requests and/or limits are not explicitly provided, the system applies cluster-wide defaults. * **If GPUs are requested** - The default CPU allocation is determined by a set ratio of CPUs per GPU. * **If no GPUs are requested** - The default CPU allocation is determined by a ratio of CPUs per CPU limit. * **If no GPUs are requested** - The default memory allocation is determined by a ratio of CPU memory limit to CPU memory request. Administrators can change cluster-wide defaults for CPU and memory requests and/or limits. * A CPU memory request with a default ratio of 200MB per GPU. * A CPU request with a default ratio of 0.1 CPUs per 1 CPU limit. * A CPU memory request with a default ratio of 0.1:1 request per CPU memory limit.

results.title: Scheduling and Resource Allocation | wiki
results.content: # wiki. View the Project on GitHub diku-dk/wiki. # Scheduling and Resource Allocation. This document describes how the cluster currently handles ressource allocations and how jobs are scheduled. The cluster schedules three resources: CPU threads, Memory and GPUs. The requested resources are guarded via cgroups: a job can allocate only as many resources as requested and can not access any other resources. CPU threads are not cores: each core offers two hyperthreads, which share the compute power of the core. Finally, to optimize runtime, slurm will try to allocate as many cores on the same physical CPU Socket as possible: this way communication between cores is fast and sharing the same L3 cache is possible. ### Job Resource Defaults. However, at maximum 8000MB memory are allocated to a single core to prevent memory-starving CPUs. This means that allocating more memory will automatically allocate more CPUs to your job, which will affect the scheduling cost (see Billing Factor below). The billing factor is how the cluster weighs the computational costs of your jobs. The billing factor and its sibling the billed seconds are central to how ressource limits and scheduling priority are computed. The runtime $T\_\text{job}$ is the actual wallclock time a job is run, not the time that was allocated for it. Just requesting an arbitrary GPU incures a billing factor of 5. This GPU might be an A100, but also one of our smaller cards. If an A100 is explicitely requested, this incurs an additional cost on your job and the resulting cost of an a100 is 15. \[F\_\text{billing} = 0.625\cdot8+5=10\]. Changing the request resources to `--gres=gpu:a100:1` results in:. \[F\_\text{billing} = 0.625\cdot8+5+10=20\]. with the output of sacct being:. allocating moe than twice the default memory (`--mem=128G`) will increase the number of cpu cores and thus the billing factor:. The fairshare factor is computed based on an exponential moving average of the consumed billing seconds. $ sshare -U -u$user -o RawUsage,NormUsage,NormShares,FairShare RawUsage NormUsage NormShares FairShare ----------- ----------- ----------- ---------- 317 1.000000 0.333333 0.333333. 1. RawUsage: the current moving average of billing seconds. 2. NormUsage: the fraction of billing seconds compared to the overall use of the cluster. 3. NormShares: the users target share of the overall available computation time.

Memory allocation strategies CPU vs GPU on deeplearning (cuda, tensorflow, pytorch,…). * When I'm running with CPU, processes take each around 500mo of CPU memory. * When I'm running with GPU, processes take each much more CPU memory (like 3Go each) and almost the same (more in reality) GPU memory. I can reduce GPU memory process fingerprint by using environment variable `TF_CUDNN_USE_AUTOTUNE=0` (1.5Go GPU, not more than 3Go CPU). But it's still much more memory consumption than running process on CPU only. When running tf process on CPU only, it uses some memory (comparable to data size). When running the same tf process on GPU only, it uses much more memory (~x16 without any tensorflow optimization). I have the same behaviour (low memory on CPU, and everything explode when running on GPU). **EDIT2 :** Some of memory allocated on GPU should be for CUDA runtime. I have 300mo memory allocated on CPU run. I have 2go of GPU memory and almost 5go of CPU memory used when running on GPU. May the main problem is the CPU/system memory allocated for this process when I'm running on GPU, since it seems that CUDA runtime can take almost 2go of GPU mem (this is huge...). Even if I try to create a 1,1 tensor with pytorch, it takes 2go of GPU and almost 5go of CPU memory. 0 GPU Memory Allocation under CUDA 8 and Pascal Architecture. 0 GPU Memory Allocation under CUDA 8 and Pascal Architecture. 2 Using CPU vs GPU to train a model - Speed vs memory. 1 Best practice for allocating GPU and CPU resources in TensorFlow. 1 Tensorflow GPU memory allocation.
